findings.title: Normal cleanup batches are logged at error level, including full ID lists
findings.body: These are expected per-batch status messages, but they use r.log.Error even when err is nil and log the full ids slice. The same pattern repeats at lines 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579. With the cleanup job running every minute, this will flood error logs and can trigger alerts, and large batch sizes may produce very large log entries listing tens of thousands of IDs. These should be debug/info logs, and full ID lists should not be logged on success.

findings.title: Cleanup job ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without explanation
findings.body: The cleanup loop now runs every minute instead of every 10 minutes, applying to all cleanup jobs: temporary files, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history. This change is unrelated to the annotation cleanup deadlock fix and is not mentioned in the PR description. It increases database load and lock contention and may make the deadlock being fixed more likely. If this was a debug leftover, it should be reverted to 10 minutes.

findings.title: deleteByIDs can exceed SQL Server's 2100-parameter limit for large batch sizes
findings.body: deleteByIDs only special-cases SQLite for parameter limits and otherwise builds an IN clause with one placeholder per ID. Microsoft SQL Server supports a maximum of 2100 parameters per statement, so configuring AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above 2100 will cause every cleanup batch on SQL Server to fail with a 'too many parameters' error. The old subquery-based delete did not bind IDs this way. The new test covers only SQLite, so this cross-database regression is not caught. The delete should be chunked or use a dialect-specific literal strategy for parameter-limited non-SQLite databases.
